findings.title: Painters keep hues close; opposites are rarer than chance
findings.sentence: Within one painting, hues 0 to 15 degrees apart sit together 1.6x as often as chance predicts; near-opposite hues (165 to 180 degrees) 0.6x.
findings.method: Every pair of distinct chromatic notes (OKLCH chroma >= .04, >= 1% of the area, OKLab distance >= .08) in each painting's 24-color pool, weighted by area x area, binned by hue difference. Null: the same notes paired with a random other painting from the same museum and century (keeps each camera's cast and each century's varnish). Ratio = observed / null. 95% interval: bootstrap over paintings.
findings.caveat: Varnish pulls every hue toward amber, which the same-museum, same-century null only partly removes.

findings.title: Partners art chooses
findings.sentence: Once each museum's and century's habits are taken out, few cross-hue pairs beat chance, and they are mostly a deep red or olive set against near-black. Strongest: Xander with Dark Jungle Green, 2.14x (n = 90).
findings.method: Each painting's pool colors named with the nearest of the ~900 core names; a name is 'present' at >= 2% of the area. Lift = paintings holding both / expected, where expected sums each museum-and-century stratum's own rates (so two colors that are merely both common in one museum's 1600s don't count). Cross-hue partners only (>= 45 deg apart, or a neutral with a hue). Kept: >= 40 paintings, OKLab distance >= .15 (two distinct colors), and a 95% Poisson interval above 1.
findings.caveat: Names are nearest-name labels of photographed color; a pair is a habit of the archive, not a rule of harmony.

findings.title: Does one color rule the canvas?
findings.sentence: The Gini index of each painting's area shares (0 = every color equal, 1 = one color is everything), median by century.
findings.method: Gini over the 24 pool shares of each painting (the pool over-clusters, so this is a relative, not absolute, measure).
findings.caveat: Dark varnished pictures merge into a few big dark clusters, which raises their Gini.

findings.title: A palette alone can date a painting
findings.sentence: From its colors alone, half of 23,129 paintings are dated within 86 years; guessing the archive's median year is off by 112.

misfits.t: Writing Books under the Pine Trees
Annunciation with Saints Maxima and Ansanus

findings.method: Features: share-weighted lightness histogram (7 bins), chroma-weighted hue histogram (8), mean chroma, mean lightness, warm share, Gini. 25-nearest-neighbor median year, 5-fold cross-validation (a painting never predicts itself).
findings.caveat: Part of what dates a picture is its varnish and the museum that photographed it, not only the painter's choices.

findings.title: Whose palette is it?
findings.sentence: Among 158 painters with 20+ works, the nearest painter-average palette names the right painter 7% of the time (top five: 21%); chance is 0.6% (top five 3.2%).
findings.method: Same 19 palette features; nearest painter centroid, leaving the painting out of its own painter's centroid.
findings.caveat: Many painters are held by one museum, so part of the 'fingerprint' is that museum's camera.

findings.title: The vertical order of color
findings.sentence: Where each color family sits on the canvas, from top to bottom: its median height, over every painting where it covers 2% or more.
findings.method: Local 200 px images (Art Institute of Chicago and SMK), frames cropped, reduced to 96 px. Each pixel gets an OKLCH family; a family's height in a painting is the mean row of its pixels (0 = top, 1 = bottom). Null: 0.5. 95% interval: bootstrap.
findings.caveat: Two museums only (Chicago and Copenhagen): Danish and American painting are over-represented.

findings.title: Light above, dark below
findings.sentence: Share of paintings whose top third is lighter than their bottom third (by more than 2 lightness points).
findings.method: Mean OKLab lightness of the top third vs the bottom third. Genre from title words (portrait / landscape words), the rest 'other'. Null: 50%.
findings.caveat: Genre from titles is rough; Danish titles are matched too.

findings.title: Lit figure, dark ground
findings.sentence: Share of portraits whose middle (where the sitter usually is) is lighter than the edges of the canvas, by era.
findings.method: Portraits by title. Center box = middle 40% across, 18-70% down; ground = the outer 12% band. Null: 50%. 95% Wilson interval.
findings.caveat: Center-weighting is a stand-in for real figure detection; old varnish darkens edges and corners more than centers.

findings.title: Warm lights, cool shadows?
findings.sentence: Share of paintings whose lightest fifth of pixels is warmer than its darkest fifth.
findings.method: OKLab a/b projected on the orange-yellow direction (60 deg); lightest 20% of pixels vs darkest 20%. Null: 50%.
findings.caveat: Yellowed varnish warms light passages most visibly, so 'warm lights' is inflated for old pictures.

findings.title: Which colors touch
findings.sentence: How often two color families share an edge, against what their areas alone predict (1.0 = chance).
findings.method: Right and down neighbor pixels with different families; expected = total neighbor pairs x area share x area share, per painting, summed.
findings.caveat: Neighbouring hues touch more partly because a soft gradient passes through them; at 96 px, brushwork blurs.

findings.title: The flesh note, century by century
findings.sentence: The average light, warm note at the center of portraits, by century.
findings.method: Portraits by title; central pixels with OKLCH hue 30-80, lightness .5-.9, chroma .03-.14 (a broad flesh band), when they cover >= 4% of the center.
findings.caveat: Varnish yellows flesh most visibly; this is photographed flesh, not mixed paint.
